summary.text: For \(k\ge 60\), set \(n=2k+1\): any nonzero matrix entry yields primes \(n+i-j\) and \(n+j-i\) whose sum is \(2n=4k+2\), so if no such prime decomposition existed the whole matrix would be zero and its determinant would vanish, contradicting the hypothesis. The remaining cases \(1\le k<60\) are settled by explicit prime-pair decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)=A228623(n)\). Thus \(a(n)\) is the determinant of the \(n\times n\) matrix \(M_n\), whose rows and columns are indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and whose \((i,j)\)-entry is
\[
(M_n)_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Here the differences are regarded as natural-number differences. For indices in the stated range they agree with the corresponding ordinary integer differences: indeed, \(j<n\le n+i\), so \(j\le n+i\), and similarly \(i\le n+j\). Consequently no truncation occurs in either difference.

Assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement
\[
\text{for every odd }n>120,\qquad a(n)\ne0.
\]
We prove that for every positive integer \(k\), the number \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

First consider the finite range \(1\le k<60\). The following table gives, for each such \(k\), primes \(p,q\) satisfying \(p+q=4k+2\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
k&(p,q)& &k&(p,q)&\\ \hline
1&(3,3)&&21&(3,83)&&41&(3,163)\\
2&(3,7)&&22&(7,83)&&42&(3,167)\\
3&(3,11)&&23&(5,89)&&43&(7,167)\\
4&(5,13)&&24&(19,79)&&44&(5,173)\\
5&(3,19)&&25&(5,97)&&45&(3,179)\\
6&(3,23)&&26&(3,103)&&46&(5,181)\\
7&(7,23)&&27&(3,107)&&47&(11,179)\\
8&(3,31)&&28&(5,109)&&48&(3,191)\\
9&(7,31)&&29&(5,113)&&49&(5,193)\\
10&(5,37)&&30&(13,109)&&50&(3,199)\\
11&(3,43)&&31&(13,113)&&51&(7,199)\\
12&(3,47)&&32&(3,127)&&52&(11,199)\\
13&(7,47)&&33&(3,131)&&53&(3,211)\\
14&(5,53)&&34&(7,131)&&54&(7,211)\\
15&(3,59)&&35&(3,139)&&55&(11,211)\\
16&(5,61)&&36&(7,139)&&56&(3,223)\\
17&(3,67)&&37&(11,139)&&57&(3,227)\\
18&(3,71)&&38&(3,151)&&58&(5,229)\\
19&(5,73)&&39&(7,151)&&59&(5,233)\\
20&(3,79)&&40&(5,157)&&&&
\end{array}
\]
For every row, direct addition gives \(p+q=4k+2\). The numbers occurring in the table are all primes; explicitly, the distinct numbers used are
\[
\begin{gathered}
3,5,7,11,13,19,23,31,37,43,47,53,59,61,67,71,73,79,83,89,97,\\
103,107,109,113,127,131,139,151,157,163,167,173,179,181,191,193,199,\\
211,223,227,229,233.
\end{gathered}
\]
Their primality is established by the elementary finite test of checking that none is divisible by a prime not exceeding its square root. This settles all \(k\) with \(1\le k<60\).

It remains to consider \(k\ge60\). Set
\[
n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd, and
\[
n=2k+1\ge121>120.
\]
The assumed nonvanishing conjecture therefore gives
\[
a(n)=\det(M_n)\ne0.
\]

We claim that this nonzero determinant yields two primes whose sum is \(4k+2\). Suppose, to the contrary, that there are no primes \(p,q\) with
\[
p+q=4k+2.
\]
Consider any row index \(i\) and column index \(j\), where \(0\le i,j<n\). Put
\[
p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i.
\]
As observed above, these natural-number subtractions are exact. Their sum is therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
p+q
  &=(n+i-j)+(n+j-i)\\
  &=2n\\
  &=2(2k+1)\\
  &=4k+2.
\end{aligned}
\]
If both \(p\) and \(q\) were prime, they would thus be a representation of \(4k+2\) as a sum of two primes, contrary to our supposition. Hence for every pair of indices \((i,j)\), at least one of \(n+i-j\) and \(n+j-i\) is not prime. By the definition of \(M_n\), every entry of \(M_n\) is consequently zero.

Thus \(M_n\) is the zero matrix. Since \(n>120\), it has positive dimension, and the determinant of this zero matrix is zero. For example, this follows immediately from the Leibniz formula for the determinant: every term is a signed product containing \(n\) matrix entries, and every such entry is zero. Therefore
\[
a(n)=\det(M_n)=0,
\]
contradicting the nonvanishing conclusion \(a(n)\ne0\).

The supposition was false. Hence when \(k\ge60\), there do exist primes \(p,q\) such that \(p+q=4k+2\). Together with the explicit finite table for \(1\le k<60\), this proves that every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is the sum of two primes.
